body:
A dental clinic in the UK now has a voice AI answering its phone. It books into the calendar. It does not do anything else.
That second part was the harder build.

What it books: new patient enquiries, reschedules, cancellations. It checks the calendar live and confirms a slot on the call, no callback needed.

What it refuses: anything clinical. "My filling hurts" gets a redirect to the practice's emergency line, not a booking. Payment questions go to voicemail marked urgent. It does not try to sound like it knows dentistry, because it doesn't.

What broke in week one: the calendar sync ran on a fifteen-minute refresh, not real time. Two callers got booked into the same 10am slot on a Tuesday because the second call came in before the first booking had synced back. The front desk caught it, but only because someone happened to look. We moved it to a webhook that fires the second a slot is taken. Should have built it that way from the start.

The other thing that surprised me: some callers hang up the moment they realise it isn't a person. Not many, but enough that we now open with a line that says exactly what it is, before it asks anything.

This is one of nine automations running inside client businesses right now. None of them started this clean.
